what: The prose says the round trip copies no bytes and the heap block never moves, but push_str in the same program grows the String from capacity 4 to 8 (a new block, bytes copied). The panel's own stepper says so.
evidence: Panel 31: "The same heap bytes made the whole round trip, and not one byte was copied." Panel 32 caption: "The heap block never moves." Stepper mem-fn step at line 9: "The String gets a bigger block, room for 8 (as in grow.rs, the bytes may move ...)". A scratch run on 1.99.1 confirms "Emma" + " OK" -> len 7, capacity 8. Same overclaim in ex-owner-trace explain ("one String, never copied": "ab"+'c' grows cap 2->8) and boss 2 explain ("the one String is never copied": "x"+'y' grows cap 1->8).
fix: Say what is true: "The moves themselves copied no text: only the 24-byte ticket record travelled. (push_str may move the bytes to a bigger block, as in grow.rs.)" Change the panel 32 caption to "The moves never touch the heap bytes." Adjust the two explains the same way ("never cloned" instead of "never copied").

what: The garbage-collector card describes Python as a janitor that walks around at unpredictable times. CPython mainly uses reference counting, which frees most objects the moment the last reference goes; only the cycle collector walks around.
evidence: "Python, Go, JavaScript and Java have a helper that walks around while your program runs, finds coats nobody holds a ticket for, and hands them back. Easy for you, but it costs time, and you can't be sure exactly when it happens."
fix: Either drop Python from the list ("Go, JavaScript and Java ...") or add "(Python mostly counts tickets instead, and has a janitor for the leftovers)".

what: "64-bit Linux, the most common kind" reads as a claim that Linux is the most common kind of computer, which is untrue for the laptops and desktops readers use.
evidence: "These sizes are for this book's computer (64-bit Linux, the most common kind). On a 64-bit Windows PC or Mac you get the same numbers."
fix: "These sizes are for this book's computer, a 64-bit Linux machine. Any 64-bit computer (almost every PC and Mac today) gives the same numbers."

what: The prompts narrow the choice to a single possible line, so the spot exercises give their answers away.
evidence: ex-spot-dangle: "Line 6 is fine. Which line uses the loan after its owner has left?" spot_dangle.rs has only one line after the block (line 8). ex-b5: "The caret points at the push on line 4 ... Which line uses a reader too late?" Only line 5 uses `host` after line 4. ex-b6 prompt: "The println! on line 6 is fine. Is line 8?"
fix: Drop the hints from the prompts ("Click the line that uses the loan after its owner has left"), or add a decoy line after the block that is innocent (for example a println! of an outer variable).

what: The prompt says the caret is on the push at line 5, and only line 6 comes after it, so the suspect is given away.

what: The explanation describes only the last printed line. The real run prints two lines, so a reader who typed both may think the first one was wrong.
